I want to write about the strange comfort of unused notebooks.

There is something almost sacred about a blank page that you haven’t yet decided what to do with. It sits there, crisp and patient, full of imagined purpose. You might use it for journaling, sketching, lists, a novel you’ll definitely start this month, or the perfect daily routine you’ll definitely follow. The notebook doesn’t argue. It simply waits.

I think unused notebooks are hopeful objects. They represent the belief that we are about to become more organized, more reflective, more creative — that a better version of us is waiting just beyond the first written line. There’s a quiet optimism in buying a notebook you don’t need, especially one with a cover that feels important in your hands.

And yet, once we begin writing, something changes. The page becomes less perfect. The handwriting is uneven. The first entry is awkward. Maybe it’s a grocery list, a complaint, a half-finished idea. The dream of the notebook collapses into the reality of being human.

But maybe that’s the point.

Maybe the purpose of the blank page was never to stay blank, beautiful, and untouched. Maybe it was there to absorb the mess. To take our scattered thoughts, our uncertain questions, our unfinished plans, and hold them without judgment. A notebook doesn’t need you to be brilliant. It only needs you to be honest.

I like that.

There’s something freeing about writing badly on purpose, about letting a sentence be ordinary, about allowing a thought to trail off before it knows where it’s going. Not everything has to be polished. Not everything has to mean something immediately. Sometimes a page is just a place where thinking can breathe.

If I had to choose one thing to write about freely, I think I would choose the small, overlooked moments that make life feel real: the way light falls across a wall in the late afternoon, the sound of rain before it actually starts, the pause between hearing a song and remembering why it matters. The ordinary is full of messages if you slow down long enough to notice them.

Maybe that’s why blank notebooks are so appealing. They remind us that attention is still possible. That we can begin again. That the next page, like tomorrow, is not asking for perfection — only presence.
